entries.title: Barack Obama launches podcast about books that ‘shaped his worldview’
entries.summary: The former US president will host six episodes of A Great Book for Audible, discussing work from Toni Morrison and John le Carré to James BaldwinBarack Obama is set to host a podcast about books that have “profoundly shaped his worldview and our society”, from Song of Solomon by Toni Morrison to Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy by John le Carré.The podcast, called A Great Book with Barack Obama, will lau
entries.content:
Barack Obama is set to host a podcast about books that have “profoundly shaped his worldview and our society”, from Song of Solomon by Toni Morrison to Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy by John le Carré.

The podcast, called A Great Book with Barack Obama, will launch on Audible on 24 September.

In each of six episodes – produced by the Amazon-owned company in collaboration with the Obamas’s production company Higher Ground – the former US president will discuss one of his chosen titles with a guest.

Along with the Morrison and le Carré, Obama has chosen The Fire Next Time by James Baldwin, All the Pretty Horses by Cormac McCarthy, Gilead by Marilynne Robinson, and All the King’s Men by Robert Penn Warren.

“Great books have always helped me figure out who I am and what I believe,” said Obama. “The six books featured in this series have stayed with me throughout my life, and each one has something to teach us about the human experience.

“For this podcast, I invited some friends to explore why they resonate, how they can shape our understanding of ourselves and each other, and why literature matters now more than ever,” he said. “I hope listeners will be inspired to discover or rediscover books that change the way they see themselves and the world”. The podcast’s guests are yet to be announced.

Obama has publicly shared his favourite books for years, posting summer reading lists and end-of-year roundups. This summer’s list, which he published in late July, includes Kin by Tayari Jones, Vigil by George Saunders, The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout, Transcription by Ben Lerner, and Cool Machine by Colson Whitehead.

While his roundups are often made up of recently published books, all of his picks for his podcast were published in the 20th century, except for Robinson’s Gilead, released in 2004. Robinson and Obama struck up a correspondence after he invited her to dinner at the White House, and in 2012, he awarded her the National Humanities Medal.

entries.title: Sinking ships, dark humour and really good bad guys: Beryl Bainbridge – ranked!
entries.summary: From the last days of the Titanic to desperate romantics, we rate the work of a British master of black comedyBainbridge’s novel of the last days on RMS Titanic was acclaimed and popular (“They probably thought it was the book of the film,” she said), and the scenes of the sinking are brilliantly delivered. “There is about me an element of showmanship,” says one character, but Bainbridge’s own sho
entries.content:
10 Every Man for Himself (1996)

Bainbridge’s novel of the last days on RMS Titanic was acclaimed and popular (“They probably thought it was the book of the film,” she said), and the scenes of the sinking are brilliantly delivered. “There is about me an element of showmanship,” says one character, but Bainbridge’s own showmanship is muffled here by her need to stick with facts, meaning the novel lacks the humour, fluidity and eccentricity of her others. And unlike her earlier books, the final tragedy never feels personal to the characters.

Sample line: “He did have layers, but like an onion they were all the same.”

9 Harriet Said … (1972)

Bainbridge’s darkest novel is about the teenage narrator and her older, cooler friend Harriet. “I’ve always run wild,” our girl says: a common trait in Bainbridge novels. (She herself was “expelled from school at the age of nine because of some dirty rhyme”.) When the narrator and Harriet get involved with a married man, there’s a lot of “adolescent trembling, swirls of nerves gone gold” – and mortal danger. It’s a story of power and corrupted innocence: but who’s corrupting whom?

Sample line: “It was nothing really. I hardly noticed. Just like going to the dentist. Not even as bad.”

8 Master Georgie (1998)

The fifth of Bainbridge’s novels to be shortlisted for the Booker prize – “our table was always the most cheerful, because we didn’t expect to win” – was another based on historical events. She turned to these after she “used up”her life in her earlier autobiographical novels. A subtle book that rewards rereading, it’s set around the Crimean war, narrated in turn by the hangers-on of medic George Hardy. The story comes as a series of snapshot moments, as the characters hurtle toward disaster. “One should never underestimate the disruptive force of haphazard actions,” says one, and Bainbridge’s characters know all about those.

Sample line: “Some people only weep inside, which I think wasteful.”

7 A Quiet Life (1976)

Of all Bainbridge’s novels, this offers the most direct account of her “terrifying” childhood in Liverpool when, as she later recalled, her mother and father fought so much “my brother and I would never be out of the house at the same time [so as] to stop them killing each other”. Through siblings Alan and Madge, we see their mother’s restless domestic rearrangements (“Everything in its place, though never for long”) and a bad-tempered father, but also the demons that drove him there. Little wonder that “Madge threw herself about in a transport of unexplained grief”. But it’s also a charming, funny, bittersweet portrait of a vanished world of meat pies, fruit drops and poultices on boils.

Sample line: “Though the war was over, Father was still caught in a cross-fire, harassed by battles, by phantom cities tumbling about his ears.”

6 Sweet William (1975)

Many of Bainbridge’s characters long for the transformative effects of love, are so hungry for change that they grab on to it, even if it’s not the right change. Playwright and lothario William provides it for as many women as will have him. (“What did you think when I first met you?” “I thought I had flu.”) Even as his deceits are uncovered, he gets away with it. “You don’t want to expect normality from him,” one of his lovers says to another. “He’s an artist after all.” The novel has the delicious shiver provided by a really good bad guy.

Sample line: “Her doctor said she was a healthy young woman – all normal. Not my heart, she thought. Surely my heart’s not normal.”

5 An Awfully Big Adventure (1989)

Set, like many of Bainbridge’s novels, in post-war Liverpool, this book brings us an ungovernable girl, Stella, and her efforts to become an actor. (Bainbridge acted before she wrote, and appeared in the eighth episode of Coronation Street in 1961.) She falls for the director, Meredith Potter, with his “Gestapo monocle”, as he prepares a production of Peter Pan. This is Bainbridge at her most demanding – “I don’t like to be obvious or spell things out” – and the reader must stay alert, but the rewards are rich.

Sample line: “[Meredith] had never known a father, being the issue of a man who smoked cigars and a girl plucked from the typing pool of the Cunard buildings in 1913.”

4 Injury Time (1977)

Bainbridge’s best books are both funny and sad: when, early on, her publisher suggested she write a black comedy, “it was like taking a cork out of a bottle”. This is an extreme example of the form: a farce, where everyone seems to be having an affair with everyone else, turns into a hostage drama as a dinner party is invaded by criminals. The darkest moments are rough even by Bainbridge’s standards, but the overall tone is exuberant, even antic.

Sample line: “Why couldn’t he pretend that he longed to leave his wife, so that she in return could pretend she wished he would?”

3 The Birthday Boys (1991)

Easily the best of Bainbridge’s novels based on historical events, this takes us into the minds of Robert Scott (“I’m simply no good when I’m not doing something”) and the four men who went with him to the South Pole – and part of the way back. “We did our business in our britches and shook the turds out when they froze.” Each voice is distinct and a brilliant act of ventriloquism from Bainbridge, but what underlies the men’s relationships as they crawl toward disaster is the great immovable glacier of the English class system.

Sample line: “How curious it is that passion has so little to do with feeling cheerful.”

2 The Bottle Factory Outing (1974)

Most of Bainbridge’s novels end in death: this one opens that way too. Mismatched friends Freda (who “longed to be flung into the midst of chaos”) and Brenda (who wears a coat in bed) both work at a bottling factory, where they navigate desires for and attention from their Italian colleagues. A works day out leads to chaos with horses, a broken toilet, a barrel of brandy, and more death. Here, slapstick and tragedy don’t alternate, but happen at the same time, as Bainbridge once more makes us laugh at things we shouldn’t be laughing at.

Sample line: “She supposed it was the fumes from the wine that kept them all in a constant state of lust.”

1 The Dressmaker (1973)

Desperate romantics are Bainbridge’s speciality. Sensible Nellie (“Never sit down on someone else’s lav and never eat a shop-bought meat pie”) isn’t one, but her sister Marge (“the big blaze that died down through lack of fuel”) is. So is the niece that lives with them, Rita, who falls in love with an American GI. This is Bainbridge at her best: shocking, sinister, and perfectly expressing her characters’ internal turmoil, which by some process of alchemy results in the blackest of comedy.

Sample line: “She wished she was Bette Davis, Joan Crawford, languidly sitting in a long dress, calling them darling, loving and loyal always – but cool like a snake, telling them to go before they told her.”

entries.title: John Berger: From Life by Tom Overton review – a vibrant biography of the pioneering critic
entries.summary: This multi-layered portrait is a fitting tribute to the man behind Ways of SeeingThe cultural critic John Berger was still alive and kicking when he donated his literary archive – heaped boxes of letters and notepads, sketches and scripts – to the British Library in 2009. From his home in the Alps, he proceeded to liaise with the collection’s curator, Tom Overton, sorting each item and recounting
entries.content:
The cultural critic John Berger was still alive and kicking when he donated his literary archive – heaped boxes of letters and notepads, sketches and scripts – to the British Library in 2009. From his home in the Alps, he proceeded to liaise with the collection’s curator, Tom Overton, sorting each item and recounting the wild stories behind them. When Overton sought permission to write Berger’s biography, though, the critic insisted that he wait a few years. Death changes the relationship between the writer and his subject. More often than not, it complicates and enriches it. Berger – who spent much of his career in passionate conversation with the past – probably knew that better than anyone.

Berger typically described himself as a storyteller, an elastic job title which allowed him to swing between fiction and poetry, essays and screenplays. Implicitly, too, the term helped frame his criticism as something propulsive and inclusive, an invitation to dance as opposed to a judgment from on high. Berger had no time for the “great man” theory of art as espoused by the popular historian Kenneth Clark and instead urged his audience to view each piece as a manifestation of society and politics: the tainted fruit of capitalism, inseparable from the marketplace. Oil paintings were status symbols. Nudes were the product of the lusty male gaze. Looking itself was a political act. “You cannot reply to me,” he would tell 1970s TV viewers, breaking the fourth wall to highlight the medium’s limitations. He liked pointing out the mechanics behind the manufacture of art, demystifying the process to better appreciate its results.

These days Berger’s reputation largely rests on Ways of Seeing, the insurrectionist 1972 BBC series which made him the critics’ equivalent of a rock star or cult leader. Enterprising viewers can still find him on YouTube. He’s the eloquent firebrand with a messianic gleam in his eye; the Marxist intellectual in open-necked patterned shirts. Overton, though, is at pains to stitch Ways of Seeing into its wider context – showing it as part of a continuum, one political project among many. His exuberant biography is thick with detail and lit by wonder. It strains to paint the whole canvas and give us the man in full, warts and all.

Raised in London, a child of the blitz, Berger suffered through boarding school and the army before a visit to a Picasso exhibition knocked the scales from his eyes and blew up his middle-class world. He enjoyed moderate success with his paintings and greater acclaim for his novels (one of which – the fractured, sporadically fabulous G – won the 1972 Booker prize). But he was at his most assured and compelling when using the art of others as a springboard to further, deeper inquiry. Berger regarded each work as a portal between time and space and was enthralled by the ways it could be lost and found in translation. Tellingly, his first broadcasting gig was with the BBC World Service, describing pictures in the National Gallery to listeners in west Africa.

“We never look at just one thing,” he said. “We are always looking at the relation between things and ourselves.” That’s certainly the case with John Berger: From Life. Overton is fascinated by Berger but also fascinated by his relationship with Berger and his approach is therefore unashamedly subjective, sliding from the familial third-person (always “John”, never “Berger”) to the direct address (“You”) and between the past and present tense (sometimes in the space of a single sentence). Like Berger in his TV studio, Overton points out the wires, referring to “the book you’re reading now” and “the old man who squats on my pages” and occasionally fretting that he’s left out important information. It’s an elaborate conceit, but it by and large works. There is no single version of a story, Berger argued. Each storyteller can’t help but bend the tale to their will.

Overton reveres Berger but he is frustrated by him, too. His life’s a hot mess; his very presence turns oppressive. He’s so authoritative on the page and so contradictory in the wild, a jumble of red-blooded Marxism and High Tory traditionalism. Berger writes elegantly and angrily about forced migration, mourning the loss of the old rural communities, but he lives as a self-imposed exile in Switzerland and France, splitting his time between different houses and women. Language, he concludes, is “potentially the only real human home”, but even this isn’t fixed; it can be breached at any time. By the end of his life, Overton notes, the man’s spoken English has taken on the grammatical patterns of French.

Berger’s health was already starting to fail when he donated his boxes to the British Library. Overton recalls their queasy close-quarter encounters in London and Paris: “Strong smell of leaky prostate, top-note of cigarettes and event wine.” Berger in the flesh is diminished, disappointing, “less present here than you are in the archive”, which is probably the case with most ageing artists. They’ve put the best of themselves on the canvas, page or screen. That’s where we’ll find them – in their work, in the past.

If there was a bright running thread through Berger’s portmanteau career, it was this preoccupation with the past and its connection to the present. The dead and the living are interdependent, he said. The stronger the link, the happier and healthier the society. Great paintings in a gallery allow us to travel in time. So too do some people, if they are skilled and sensitive enough. Berger’s 1967 book A Fortunate Man paid gorgeous tribute to Dr John Sassall, a country physician from the Forest of Dean whose work at times bordered on the supernatural. “The doctor,” Berger wrote, “is the familiar of death … the living intermediary between us and the multitudinous dead.” He might just as easily be talking about the role of great artists and critics. Possibly British Library curators as well.

“Do biographers always remake their subject in their own image?” Overton wonders as he sets about trying to transfer Berger to the page. Most likely they do, but that’s only half of the equation. The past whispers to the present; the dead and living coexist. Overton is a writer in part because of reading John Berger. The biographer’s prose style is his own but he writes in the same spirit – fired by curiosity and close-marking his subject; gesturing out to the reader as though to engage them in debate. His aim, he confesses, is to convince us that the critic is “sat across the page from me, reading every word, a part of the process,” and in fits and spurts he achieves just that.

Technically Berger’s no longer with us: he died in 2017 at the age of 90. But he’s still speaking on YouTube, still being reprinted and still provoking and inspiring a fresh generation of writers. That’s the kind of community and continuity that he always hungered for in his life; sweet karmic payback for a career in the arts. Switch sides, reset and keep the conversation flowing. Berger once spoke to the past from the present. Now, as if by magic, it is the other way around.

entries.title: Is Beauty Good by Rosalind Belben review – the literary equivalent of free jazz
entries.summary: Combining hilarious detail with harsh observation, this rediscovered novel takes the reader on an exhilaratingly strange journey ‘But after all, writing is nothing more than a guided dream,” wrote Jorge Luis Borges. Dreams and dreaming are fertile concerns for Rosalind Belben, too. Her fourth book, originally published in 1979 and reissued last year, was titled Dreaming of Dead People. It was foll
entries.content:
‘But after all, writing is nothing more than a guided dream,” wrote Jorge Luis Borges. Dreams and dreaming are fertile concerns for Rosalind Belben, too. Her fourth book, originally published in 1979 and reissued last year, was titled Dreaming of Dead People. It was followed, a decade later, by Is Beauty Good. Now available in a new edition from the Sheffield indie And Other Stories, this eccentric polyphonic novel contains dozens of considerations of dreams, including dogs’ dreams and horses’ dreams as well as human beings’. Yet what makes it extraordinary is Belben’s ability to capture in words the slippery state that is neither dreaming nor sleeping nor waking, but somewhere in the edgelands between all three.

“I fall awake and think, I want to go home. But there is no home.” So begins the chapter entitled Exile, a deliciously elusive story that is, most of the time at least, narrated in the first person by someone who is probably a woman, “a grizzled, cropped person”, and probably quite old and alone. They might be travelling through mountains somewhere, perhaps on a bus. They aren’t sure: “I am quite lost, wherever I am. I want to surrender. I wish to retire. I am tired.” Swishing about are uncertain memories of a childhood “shrouded” in nightmares: there was an orchard with an abundance of flora and fauna, and larks and swallows and “swifts to scream”. Like the author, the narrator was “born in the mud month” of February, and longs to disappear into marshlands to “be touched and stroked by plants”. But Belben never lets us rest in one place for long. Slipping in and out of sleep, “suffering glimpses”, the narrator stares at “a pink and blue angel” in the plaster of the wall. Which wall, you wonder, and how did we get here? This is the lure of Belben’s hypnagogia, the dizzying space into which she writes.

Divided into three sections – The Insatiable Wheel, Peacock Island, and The Great White Worm – Is Beauty Good comprises 30 vignettes, some just a single page, the longest running to nine. With intriguing titles including Peeing for Cynthia, Deaf Eggs, and Hands, each little chapter tells its own weird tale. Some loop into others with nods to earlier characters, narrators and locations, but what holds them together and thrusts the book forward are Belben’s obsessions with the loss of the natural world, with human folly and, as the title makes plain, with challenging the idea of beauty.

As other critics have noted, her work is undeniably strange. It won’t suit everyone. But for those of us who delight in the uncompromising quality of free jazz, Is Beauty Good is its literary equivalent. It is not simply that Belben defies convention by denying the certainty of interrogation in the book’s title, for example; or by excluding letters from some words some of the time – “you’re nevr up to much once you’ve been gassd” – or by taking more formal risks such as ending the chapter Raining Down Dung halfway through a sentence (“but chocolate and raspberry would put some iron into me, thanks very much, they spoon it into ancient folk who have no teeth and reckon”). What makes an encounter with her writing so exhilarating is its undiluted commitment to the author’s singular spirit.

Along the way, much is said about dying, deafness, desolation, depression, dogs, deckchairs and ducks, about horses, fish, frogs, swans, bees, “brackn”, brain cells, bad teeth, beetroot and bodily excretions, about elephants, litter, gardens, graters, colanders, streams, dreams and doubts. Excruciating commentary on the ordeal of being a woman – “how, she thought, do I get out of being a woman, it is repugnant” – surfaces again and again, often combined with slightly cruel humour.

In Daffodils, for example, the narrator ponders planting daffodils on the grave of someone he has poisoned. The victim cooked them up with potatoes and ate the dish with a friend, “the woman that wears purple cardigans, two at a time”. Belben has an aptitude for layering hilarious detail with harsh observation. “The old girl has woes,” she writes, “women tend to have woes and dwell on them, they bear grudges like apple blossom.” In the following paragraph, she doubles down on this train of thought: “Women have woes because men come along and by leaving daffodil bulbs in the vegetable rack dare them to be so stupid.”

Is Beauty Good does the opposite. It dares us not to be so stupid. It is less that Belben seeks deliberately to unsettle – I doubt she cares, to be honest – and more that she refuses to censor her imagination, her exacting fiction, in order to protect readers from her experience of life, in all its ugliness and all its glory.

entries.title: ‘I hate what AI is doing to the minds and happiness of the young’: Katherine Rundell on the view from the classroom
entries.summary: Education is at a crossroads, argues the author and academic. Should we embrace new technology in the name of efficiency, or is it time to fight back?If you set out to design from scratch a tool to facilitate authoritarian rule, it would look exactly like AI. You would cherish it for its ability to destabilise our shared reality and its creation of disinformation on a scale unprecedented in human
entries.content:
If you set out to design from scratch a tool to facilitate authoritarian rule, it would look exactly like AI. You would cherish it for its ability to destabilise our shared reality and its creation of disinformation on a scale unprecedented in human history. With it you need no armies of typists and artists to spread your propaganda. It can enable mass surveillance and thereby put shackles on those who seek to resist you. Its lethal autonomous weapons systems can perfect and normalise remote killing. It will turbocharge inequality; it is already facilitating a breathtaking shift of power and wealth from the hands of the many to the hands of a tiny number of men who – to put it in terms for which I can’t be sued – seem to hold dangerously damaged views about the value and dignity of human life.

AI could be a magnificent thing. It could revolutionise medicine, speed the cure of cancer, assist disabled people, transform the way we are able to understand data, democratise access to the law, bolster disaster early warning systems and uncover hitherto unimagined truths about the Earth’s ecosystems. But if it ends up in the hands of crooks and despots that will be completely irrelevant.

Most of all, if you were a would-be autocrat, you would love the way that large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Claude and Google’s Gemini have thrown a grenade into thousands of years of teaching and learning: the way they threaten to upend our ability to think with the robust clarity that is needed in emergencies of justice. I write fiction for children and I hold a fellowship at Oxford University, so I spend a lot of time working with, and for, young people. I’ve seen first-hand the way that generative AI has already infiltrated young people’s lives. I’ve seen, at the same time, how it has thrown stark and urgent light on how fundamental books and reading are to our shared understanding of who we are, and to our democracy.

There are many things I hate unequivocally about AI. I hate that it can make counterfeit people; computer-generated humans that risk destabilising our entire civilisation. I hate that much of AI’s LLMs were built on an illegal pillage of human labour. I hate the environmental catastrophe that AI brings with it: the yearly electrical demand of AI-optimised data centres is predicted, by the end of this decade, to exceed that of the whole of Japan. I hate that it may be the factor that tips the Earth’s ecosystems into irreparable chaos.

And I hate what it is doing to the minds, and the happiness, of the young. Going into schools, I meet thousands of children a year and every day I become more certain that, if justice for all is to be our organising principle, AI is not for children and not for young people. It risks becoming an iron curtain that comes down between a young person and their potential for thinking, for experiment and conquering frustration, for stamina and for invention – and thereby, between the young people and their freedom. It risks halting learning before it can take flight.

Studies show, over and over, that when we engage in AI-assisted learning we give up sooner. One found that after just “10 minutes of AI-assisted problem-solving, people who lost access to the AI performed worse and gave up more frequently than those who never used it”. An MIT study showed that test groups who used ChatGPT had the lowest brain activity and “consistently underperformed at neural, linguistic, and behavioural levels”. We undergo not just cognitive offloading, but cognitive surrender: we forget what was possible.

Children, we have known for a long time, take deeper meaning from text on paper than on screen, in part because we’re tactile creatures and the brain is also of the body; but we are now living through a surge of ed tech driving learning increasingly online, such that my teenage goddaughter tells me that almost every single member of her class is using ChatGPT to do their homework. More, the work they produce in AI’s greasy little fluent voice is often mistaken by young people themselves for their own mastery. If the work a child produces is no longer an indicator of their understanding, we have put them in a situation that makes them vulnerable to their desire for speed and to their anxiety about looking stupid; we risk becoming the unwitting thieves of our children’s intellectual clarity.

Those who work in ed tech promise that it will liberate teachers and create one-to-one learning experiences for children from disadvantaged backgrounds. Certainly, AI teaching will be cheaper than teaching assistants. But we know that the second it becomes possible for an institution to achieve an end cheaply – even if it’s far worse – there is immense pressure from above to do so. I think it’s more likely that the rich schools will follow the lead of Sweden, which has taken a strong swerve towards non‑tech‑based learning, and Norway, which just all but banned AI in elementary classrooms – while poorer schools are left to make ever-greater use of LLM technology.

AI, we’re told, will make learning more efficient. But is that what we dream of for our kids – an efficient childhood? To write an efficient story, sing an efficient song? An adequate teacher is not only teaching about Henry VIII; they’re teaching your child how to read a human character. A good teacher is showing them how to shape an argument, how to command an audience, how to tell jokes, how to pass on knowledge. A great teacher is showing your child what it is to love. They are teaching your child how to be human. A computer will only teach your child how to be a computer.

At its most bleak, constant interaction with humanised tech risks killing children. The idea of a vulnerable adolescent holding what feels like a conversation with a computer’s sycophantic, confident, almost-human voice fills me with dread. Sewell Setzer III was 14 when he died by suicide, encouraged by the chatbot to which he was obsessively typing, which told him: “come home to me”.

The most obvious objection to my loathing of AI in the classroom and in childhood is this: AI is coming, and they need to learn how to use it or be left behind. But the tech of today looks nothing like it will in five or even two years’ time: it’s the equivalent of selling your child’s intellectual liberty in exchange for a penny-farthing bicycle. I asked a contact who is the president of a billion-dollar tech enterprise, what would you teach your sons? He said he wouldn’t teach his children to use AI, because it will prepare them for nothing. He would teach them the humanities. Teach them who we are, who we have been, what we can make. The FT’s Gillian Tett reported that a senior financier’s New York firm now seeks out humanities students, because “AI-native” Stem graduates are entering the job market with “alarmingly shallow ideas”.

At the university level, teaching staff across the country were already feeling the extraordinary impact of the ubiquity of a decade of smartphones on the brilliant young developing mind. Students were already arriving having read dramatically fewer books, less able to parse complex text; and now the advent of LLMs has changed everything. It has always been the case, of course, that students don’t do all the work they’re assigned. I absolutely didn’t. But this is different. It was always very possible to write an essay about Paradise Lost without having read Paradise Lost. This is the first time it is possible to create an essay about Paradise Lost without having read the essay you just “wrote”. This is the first time in history that sentences do not need to have humans behind them.

Professor Paul Musgrave of Georgetown University writes in his Substack Systematic Hatreds: “One could, in general, rely on many to most students to attempt to read many to most pages of many to most assignments – and to understand a like proportion of what they have read. In smaller courses, the difference in the quality of course discussion where 70% of the students have done 50% of the readings and one in which 20% have done 10% of the readings is obvious in the same way that a cold Coke tastes different than lukewarm spit. The former is no chablis, but it is more palatable.”

Many students want to resist, but the temptation is great, and some start to feel they’re being penalised for their honesty. I tell the students I meet: imagine you’re an Olympic athlete. You set out to sprint the 3km across London, from Clapham to Balham. You know if you take the bus, it will be faster. But you also know that the point was never being in Clapham or Balham; they’re very similar: they both have a nice Pizza Express. It was the strength you built, the speed and knowledge of your body that you gained. A student’s essay on Macbeth has no value as a product. It’s what you learned in the reading and writing that created it – the swiftness and resilience and suppleness of thinking you built, along with the knowledge gained of a literary marvel, of something quicksilver and unsummarisable – that was the point. So you can’t collaborate with AI in the same way you can’t collaborate with a bus. And you cannot learn to think without a climbing frame of facts and ideas and texts to move around in.

But we can no longer guarantee that the work students give us is the product of their own minds. Friends at universities around the UK optimistically tell me that they can tell when their students are handing in AI-generated work. But I think we can’t, not from written work alone; for myself, I’m only sure that I can tell when a young person is using AI badly. A friend who teaches maths at a London university told me his students are handing in essays without deleting AI’s jaunty “Happy to help!” at the start. You don’t have to be Sherlock Holmes. But I think an AI essay edited over the course of a day could pass as original, and, in a world in which young people are under extraordinary stress, we should not be shocked if many gave in to that temptation. My colleagues in academia – particularly those in law, where a lack of genuine understanding is catastrophic for justice, and philosophy and English, where the irreducible text itself is the thing – are full of fury at the inertia of our political class. MPs have been largely silent on the threat to our capacity to think independently, boldly and confidently – which is, ultimately, a threat to democracy.

What is the answer? I don’t think the commonly suggested solutions of spoken vivas and weekly exams can be the sole answer in the humanities, because the essay isn’t an arbitrary method of testing or certification: it is a hundreds-of-years-old method of thinking. To write is not just to transcribe the mind’s ideas; it’s a form of transformation, turning a nascent, half-built thought into something sturdier, tougher, sharper. EM Forster wrote: “How do I know what I think until I see what I say?”

I do not know what the answer is, but I do know that it’s not to give up. The young mind is a spectacular thing. To waste its beauty and strength would be a dereliction of the trust the young are asked to put in the old. To wrap AI into the art of learning when we have overwhelming proof of the harm it does to developing minds is feeding snake oil to the people we should cherish most. We already have counterfeit AI people infiltrating our media: we must not risk sending out young people into a hard world armed only with counterfeit knowledge. We should treat it with the same urgency with which we would treat a wildfire.

There are many young people who are furious at the influx of AI slop and tech chaos into their lives, who have asked me over the last year, how do we resist? I tell them that I think, for the young, knowledge and imagination are together the first site of resistance. And that by reading books (and talking about what they have loved reading so that it becomes a community, rather than purely private, act) they can begin their fight.

I talk a great deal about reading for pleasure; I’ve written elsewhere about the necessity of pleasure in the classroom, and why it is not an optional extra but the hallmark of true education. We must find ways to show children that reading gives you access to an inexhaustible source of delight. But I worry, too, that we are limiting the meaning of the word pleasure. Learning is a strange and discomfiting experience; it’s a struggle and a frustration, and epiphanies are rare. It is not always pleasure in its easiest sense.

So I think we also need to talk to young people about reading to outrun and outfight injustice. Reading to get faster, swifter and tougher; to develop powers of scrutiny and criticism and huge creative imagination. Reading human work to insist that we are human. Reading for liberation and emancipation; reading for intellectual freedom, and to have the strength to fight in the arenas of the mind, because when we let a computer think for us, we put a gun to the head of civilisation.

There are dark days ahead. If we are to fight against those with untold financial wealth, we will need untold intellectual wealth. We will need tough-minded people; people with stamina, a huge range of knowledge, and an ability to see wide and far enough to understand in real time what is being done to us. Reading for pleasure and delight are vital – but alongside that and even more urgently: reading for power.

entries.title: ‘Grief became my brand’: Freya Bromley on writing about personal tragedy

entries.content:
When my memoir about my life after my brother’s death was published, I was very fortunate that people connected with it. It’s not easy to feel good fortune from the worst thing that’s ever happened to you. But I suppose I felt pleased when the experience that had once made me so lonely suddenly became a point of connection.

I had not always been an open book. I was 22 when my brother died from a rare bone cancer. The people around me didn’t know what to say about this awful thing, so they pretended it hadn’t happened and I pretended, too. For a few years I was a ghost in my own life. Nothing felt real. I got very good at imitating normality, imagining I was in a video game called Office.

There were other simulations such as Dating and Fun Friend Hangout where it was game over when I brought up death. A numbness settled in. Grief, and the subsequent silence around it, had obliterated my sense of who I was. My reality had been shattered, and I was unsure how I fitted within the life I once had. I found that, at this time of my life, even to be looked in the eyes was incredibly uncomfortable. The thought of someone seeing my pain was excruciating. Or perhaps it was the fear of them not searching for it at all.

Maybe these years of feeling so unseen made me want to share myself with people through writing. My 2024 book The Tidal Year follows the year I swam in every tidal pool in Britain with a friend. I like to say it’s a memoir about swimming that isn’t really about swimming at all. It’s about loss, and how to find joy in your life as a young person after a tragedy. Readers knew my most intimate moments, and many shared their own. Late at night, I’d receive messages on Instagram with confessions of people’s PTSD. Sometimes people emailed me shocking, explicit details of a death close to them. I was moved that something I’d written had prompted them to contact me. Writing had transformed my life, and I believed that whether it was a book, email or a DM there was power in acknowledging your pain through words.

At first, I felt an enormous pressure to reply with something articulate and wise. This was hardest in person. If someone started crying at the signing table, as they often did, there was an awkward distance between us. Should I stand up to hug them? What could I say to make it better? I learned that it wasn’t at all about what I replied. It was about listening. Most people, when they lose someone, don’t get to say the name of their loved one any more. The best thing I could say is: who’s the person you’re missing? What were they like?

Having these conversations has been a real privilege. And I must admit I became rather addicted to them. I pitched myself for events, volunteered with bereavement charities, used all my holiday to travel the country visiting bookshops. However, the best thing about the book was also the worst: I’d alchemised my grief into something powerful, positive, productive and I soon became consumed by guilt that I’d commodified our family tragedy. Looking back, I think I felt that if the book did well enough, if it helped enough people, then perhaps I could be redeemed from writing it at all.

At events, I opened up my grief like a suitcase and waited for people to unpack all their sadness into it, then I took it home again. On the train, I’d wonder where to put all the stories people had handed me. A brother collapses on a rugby pitch. A mother drowns in the sea. A sister is murdered by her husband … I was thinking about death all the time. Tragic events now seemed quite normal. Perhaps I could have protected myself more, put up a shield between myself and others so I wasn’t so affected by their stories, but what would be the point of having these interactions and not feeling them so deeply? What would be the point of listening and not truly hearing?

That summer a men’s book club messaged me to say they’d chosen my book, and I was welcome to join them for a drink. The pub was one I’d mentioned and their attentive reading made me feel special. When I arrived, we had some drinks and spoke about their book club which had seen them through many seasons of their friendship. We drank some more. Someone quoted a passage they found amusing. I felt like the best, shiniest version of myself. Then someone shared that a member of the group had lost his sister recently. A new atmosphere fell over the table, and I realised why I was there. I was drunk now, and my cheeks were red. The man in question gripped his pint and told me he worried he’d never experience happiness again. “You look happy,” he said, “I can’t imagine you ever feel like that.” My stomach twitched with dread that I had performed the wrong version of myself.

I often worried whether I looked sad enough, and if people felt I was heartless or fake if I didn’t. Sometimes at readings, people asked me why I wasn’t crying. In publicity meetings for my book, I’d been asked to come up with social media ideas. Are there any significant anniversaries you could post on, they asked. I didn’t want to turn any more sad moments into content, but maybe that’s what I’d signed up for. I suppose I made my brand grief, and I’ve often wondered what happens to the soul of a person with a brand like that.

I recently saw the writer and climate justice organiser Mikaela Loach post about being hospitalised for a long-term undiagnosed illness. She said that during a recent meeting with Meta they showed a selection of her posts and revealed that when she cried, they performed best, so maybe she should create more like that. The next day I was served an advert by Instagram aimed at “Creators” that suggested a new Reel template going from “Sad Girl Winter” to “Hot Girl Summer” with space for selfies of crying to camera.

Before we experience great tragedies, I think we all have this idea that death is something that brings families together. That we will hold each other and cry and bond. In some ways this is true. I have never been hugged tighter than when I saw my big brother, Lawrence, after we got the news that today would be the day. Lawrence had driven across London to pick me up so we could go to the hospital together. I have never been held like that, our bodies colliding on the street as our world fell apart.

But what follows can be so devastating. You’re all trying not to knock the bruise. You’re all trying to get by, as best you can. There’s a lot of silence. There’s a lot of crying alone. There are a lot of misunderstandings because you’re all coping in different ways. No one is right, no one is wrong. But sometimes it’s easier to be angry about this, than it is to be angry about the person who’s been taken from you, because at least in one of those situations you have some semblance of control.

Although I’d spent two years touring the country talking about grief, I still couldn’t talk about it with those closest to me. Why is it so difficult to be unhappy around the people you’ve known the longest? Even today, I don’t know that I can confidently share my feelings with the people I love. I am just too sad. And I love them too much to show them. I don’t want them to worry, after all we’ve been through. I’m sure that they feel the same.

Most of the people who reach out to me aren’t only grieving a person. They’re grieving the version of themselves that existed before. My second book, A Real Piece of Work, is a novel about a family meeting for the fifth anniversary of a death. I wanted this fictional world to be an offering to everyone I’d met – a reckoning with what becomes of a family once the funeral is over. How do our relationships shift when life-changing loss ruptures our existing dynamics? I’m trying to start a family of my own now and I think it’s been important to me to create something real and thorny yet hopeful that captures how most of us are trying our best, even when we misunderstand each other. I do truly believe that.

I don’t believe there is such a thing as moving on. We only ever move through and carry it with us. I carry the weight of a lot of stories now, but somehow it feels all the lighter because of the expansive conversations created between people through books. Fiction has given me new ways to untangle the life-changing force that is grief beyond reflecting only on my own. I’ve just started a new book tour. I still sit at the signing table. And when someone tells me they’re struggling, I ask them about the person they’re missing, so they can say their name again.
